days.review: After learning something once, memory can drop steeply — Ebbinghaus showed you might fall from high retention toward very little within a day. That decay eventually hits everything. Today you measure what survived from your own recent study so spacing has a personal baseline, not an abstract graph.

task.do: Pick material you studied 1–2 days ago and have not reviewed. Closed-book, write what you still remember (5 min). Check notes and estimate % retained. Note what vanished first — about 8 minutes.
task.capture: Topic, rough % retained, and 3 items that disappeared.

check.q: Using your retention estimate after a delay, how should you read that drop in light of the forgetting curve — as a personal failure, or as expected data?
check.rubric: correct: Sharp drop after one exposure is normal baseline; spacing exists to slow later fades — not a verdict on ability. mostly_correct: Accepts some forgetting without linking to spacing. incorrect: Any drop means abandon subject; perfect memory should be default.
check.exemplar: My modest retention is expected decay after one exposure, not proof I cannot learn. It is baseline data spacing is meant to fight by slowing the next fade.

check.q: Looking at the three items that vanished first, what is the best immediate use of that list?
check.rubric: correct: Target them with active recall in the next spaced review. mostly_correct: Study them again vaguely. incorrect: Ignore and reread everything equally; highlight-only; recognition glances only.
check.exemplar: Those three items should be the targets for active recall in my next spaced review — not buried in an undifferentiated full-chapter reread.

check.q: If low retention felt demoralizing, what is a productive framing that still leads to action?
check.rubric: correct: Expected decay data to fight with spaced, high-quality retrieval — not quit testing or only cram forever. mostly_correct: Stay hopeful without naming spacing action. incorrect: Spacing useless because forgetting happened; stop testing to avoid seeing losses.
check.exemplar: Low retention is expected decay data I can fight with well-timed, high-quality retrieval. Stopping tests so I never see losses would only hide the problem.

days.review: Each well-timed review makes the memory fade *more slowly* next time — the spacing effect, one of the most valuable tools in learning. Massing everything in one sitting feels productive; spreading retrieval over time changes the slope of forgetting. Today you schedule real reviews on your own calendar.

task.do: Choose 2 topics you need long-term. On your calendar/planner, place a short active-recall review for each at three future times (e.g., +1 day, +1 week, +1 month — adjust to your term). Keep each block 10–15 minutes — about 8 minutes to plan.
task.capture: Paste the two topics with their three dated review slots.

check.q: Look at the schedule you just made. What about it actually uses the spacing effect rather than massed study?
check.rubric: correct: Multiple retrieval sessions spread over days/weeks for the same topics. mostly_correct: Mentions reviewing later vaguely. incorrect: One marathon tonight; anxiety rereads; infinite new material with no revisits.
check.exemplar: I have three retrieval sessions for each topic spread across days and weeks. That distributed retrieval is spacing — not one 3-hour marathon tonight.

check.q: A friend crams the same topic for four hours today instead of using spaced slots. What trade-off should you expect between their plan and yours?
check.rubric: correct: Cramming may feel strong now but fades faster; spaced reviews slow later forgetting. mostly_correct: Prefers spacing without fade trade-off. incorrect: Cramming always beats spacing long-term; spaced plan weaker because less intense today.
check.exemplar: Their cram may feel stronger today, but it should fade faster. My spaced retrievals should make the memory fade more slowly next time even if today feels less intense.

check.q: Which calendar entry from today is strongest, and how would you rewrite a vague "study more" entry to match that standard?
check.rubric: correct: Dated blocks with topic + active recall; vague intentions need topic + retrieval method + date. mostly_correct: Wants dates without retrieval specificity. incorrect: Only exam-eve cram; "look at notes" with no retrieval.
check.exemplar: My dated blocks labeled with topic and active recall are strongest. "Study more" should become a specific date, topic, and closed retrieval method.

days.review: You do not need fancy software. A solid default: review after **1 day, then 1 week, then 1 month.** Exact intervals are not critical — 3 hours vs a day, or 3 weeks vs 6 weeks, can all work. Consistency matters, and *what you do* in each review matters more than the algorithm.

task.do: Pick one concept you learned today (or yesterday). Write a mini plan on paper: Review A tomorrow (free recall), Review B in ~1 week (varied cues), Review C in ~1 month (exam-style use). Put the first reminder in your phone now — about 8 minutes.
task.capture: Concept name + the three review dates/actions you chose.

check.q: If you agonized over 6 vs 8 days for Review B, what does the lesson say you should prioritize instead?
check.rubric: correct: Consistency and quality of spaced retrieval over exact interval tuning. mostly_correct: Says don't stress dates vaguely. incorrect: Only perfect algorithms work; must review every hour.
check.exemplar: Exact tuning matters little compared with consistently doing quality spaced retrieval. Obsessing over 6 vs 8 days is the wrong lever.

check.q: How do your three reviews reflect the day / week / month default spirit rather than massing or a single pass?
check.rubric: correct: Expanding gaps across day/week/month scales with retrieval actions. mostly_correct: Lists three reviews without naming expanding gaps. incorrect: All three tonight; only one review ever; passive rereads only.
check.exemplar: I spread retrieval across tomorrow, about a week, and about a month with different retrieval modes. That expanding-gap default is not massing all three into tonight.

check.q: If your phone reminder only says "study," how should you improve it after today's task?
check.rubric: correct: Specify concept + closed-book retrieve how. mostly_correct: Make it more specific vaguely. incorrect: Delete reminders; replace with reread everything; fifty same-night alarms.
check.exemplar: I should name the concept and that I will retrieve closed-book. A vague "study" reminder does not make the spacing action concrete.

days.review: The research does *not* show that a perfectly tuned interval matters much. The quality of the retrieval session matters far more: active recall that hits an integrated schema and "practices how you play." A mediocre app interval with weak recognition flipping loses to a simple schedule with strong production.

task.do: Run one scheduled (or overdue) review on your own material for ~8 minutes: closed integrated recall or exam-style use — no answer-peeking first. Avoid isolated recognition glances. End by noting whether the session trained how you will be tested.
task.capture: What you retrieved, how (free/cued/problem), and one upgrade to make next review more exam-real.

check.q: Describe the review session you just ran. What made it higher or lower quality by this lesson's standard?
check.rubric: correct: Judges by production before checking / integrated or exam-like use vs recognition nodding or interval tinkering only. mostly_correct: Calls it good/bad without quality criteria. incorrect: Perfect app timing alone = high quality.
check.exemplar: Mine was higher quality because I produced an integrated answer before checking. Flipping cards and nodding at familiar answers — even at a "perfect" interval — would have been low quality.

check.q: If an app buzzed at the "perfect" time but you only recognized answers, what should you prioritize fixing?
check.rubric: correct: Generation-before-check and exam-real tasks — timing cannot rescue recognition-only. mostly_correct: Mentions trying harder vaguely. incorrect: Buy a better algorithm; ignore quality because timing was perfect.
check.exemplar: I should fix generation-before-check and make tasks more exam-real. Perfect timing does not rescue recognition-only reviews.

check.q: Which upgrade in your capture best aligns with "practice how you play," and why?
check.rubric: correct: Swap definition glances for problem/explain-as-tested retrieval. mostly_correct: Mentions an upgrade without exam-real link. incorrect: More identical easy stems; shorten intervals to minutes today; remove production.
check.exemplar: Swapping pure definition glances for problem or explain-as-tested retrieval aligns with practice how you play — it trains the performance I need, not only comfortable recognition.

days.review: Each new flashcard commits your future self to many repetitions. One lecture might spawn 30–50 cards → ~150 reviews; several lectures a day → hundreds stacking next week while new cards arrive. That compounding pile is *learning debt*, and motivated students often drown by week two. Today you audit your own backlog.

task.do: If you use cards (or a to-review list), count new items from the last 3–5 study days and estimate pending reviews this week. If you do not use cards, count "things I meant to restudy" instead. Mark whether the pile is growing — about 8 minutes.
task.capture: Numbers: new items, estimated pending reviews, and one sentence on whether debt is rising.

check.q: If your pending reviews are rising while you keep adding cards (or restudy items), what pattern is that — and why is high motivation not a fix by itself?
check.rubric: correct: Learning debt compounding toward collapse; motivation can accelerate adding debt. mostly_correct: Sees backlog problem vaguely. incorrect: Proof spacing scales forever; add cards faster; debt irrelevant if motivated.
check.exemplar: That is learning debt compounding toward collapse. High motivation can make it worse if I keep adding items faster than I repay reviews.

check.q: You estimated a large future-rep load from one dense lecture's cards. What is the best response?
check.rubric: correct: Shrink what becomes a card; invest more in encoding so fewer reps needed. mostly_correct: Make fewer cards vaguely. incorrect: Keep generating that volume; ignore math; stop all review forever.
check.exemplar: I should shrink what becomes a card and invest more in encoding so I need fewer spaced reps — not celebrate a huge deck from every lecture.

check.q: Which detail in your capture is the clearest early warning of unsustainable spacing, and what would a healthier pattern look like?
check.rubric: correct: Pending reviews growing week over week vs a small stable finishable list. mostly_correct: Mentions numbers without growth warning. incorrect: Rising backlog is fine; only rereading with no list is healthier.
check.exemplar: Pending reviews growing week over week is the clearest warning. A healthier pattern is a small stable deck or list I actually finish daily.

days.review: Spacing alone has a second problem: answering isolated cards keeps you at low, isolated mastery, so complex integrated problems still wreck you no matter how many reps you log. Flashcards can support memory; they do not replace building connected understanding. Today you stress-test a "known" card cluster with an integrated task.

task.do: Take 5–8 cards/facts you can answer in isolation from your subject. Put them away. On a blank page, write an integrated explanation or solve a mixed problem that requires using several together — 7–8 minutes, then check.
task.capture: Which isolated items you "knew," and where the integrated attempt broke.

check.q: If you hit every card but failed the integrated task, what does that mean about isolated mastery?
check.rubric: correct: Isolated mastery is not enough for complex performance. mostly_correct: Admits a gap without naming isolation limit. incorrect: More identical card reps auto-fix integration; integrated tasks unfair.
check.exemplar: It means isolated mastery is not enough. I can ace atomic cards and still fail when complex performance needs the ideas connected.

check.q: What adjustment should your review plan make after today's break — without abandoning spacing?
check.rubric: correct: Add periodic closed integrated retrieval, not only atomic cards. mostly_correct: Mentions synthesis vaguely. incorrect: Only easier cards; stop spacing; replace checks with highlighting.
check.exemplar: I should keep spacing but add periodic closed integrated explain/problem sessions on the same cluster — not only atomic flips.

check.q: Write a healthy study-log line for a session like today's, and contrast it with a misleading "40 cards correct" line.
check.rubric: correct: Combines modest cards + closed integrated work; contrasts with cards-only or peeking recognition. mostly_correct: Wants integration mentioned vaguely. incorrect: Celebrates card count with skipped synthesis as healthy.
check.exemplar: A healthy line is "15 cards + one closed integrated explain on the same cluster." "40 cards correct; skipped synthesis" would hide the shallow-mastery problem I just saw.

days.review: Relying only on active recall + spaced repetition is a *rate-limiting step*: like a short plank in a barrel, learning leaks from the weakest part. Pair spacing with strong encoding. Encode well and the forgetting curve flattens, so you need far fewer repetitions — Justin's example: a heavy master's topic needing only ~10–15 cards after good encoding.

task.do: Choose a topic whose card count or review load feels heavy. Spend ~8 minutes building/improving a one-page big-picture keyword map (relationships, not a transcript). Then list cards you could delete or never make because the map already holds them.
task.capture: Map summary (groups/links) and a prune list of cards/items you no longer need as isolates.

check.q: You pruned cards after mapping. What principle about encoding and spaced reps did you apply?
check.rubric: correct: Better encoding reduces how many spaced reps you need; spacing supports encoding rather than replacing it. mostly_correct: Says maps help reduce cards vaguely. incorrect: More cards always beat encoding; maps replace all retrieval forever.
check.exemplar: Stronger encoding flattens forgetting so I need fewer spaced reps. Spacing supports that encoding — it does not replace building the big picture.

check.q: If your deck is huge and integrated questions still fail, what is the highest-leverage move?
check.rubric: correct: Invest in encoding/big picture, not only more reps. mostly_correct: Mentions understanding vaguely. incorrect: Double daily cards; shorten every interval to minutes; avoid maps to save time.
check.exemplar: Highest leverage is investing in encoding and the big picture. Doubling card count keeps leaning on the short plank instead of fixing it.

check.q: Which kind of item on your prune list is safest to cut, and which kinds should you keep?
check.rubric: correct: Cut isolates the map already explains; keep items that still fail in exam-style/conditional/integrated use. mostly_correct: Cuts something redundant vaguely. incorrect: Cut core failing procedures/gaps; keep only saturated wording clones.
check.exemplar: Safest cuts are isolated wordings I can already explain through the map's relationships. I keep procedures or conditional distinctions I still fail in real use.

days.review: Flashcards are great when aligned with your goal — best for Reference and some Evidence information (PACER). Keep decks small, keep cards spaced, vary cues, and always retrieve before flipping. Overwhelm or stuck low mastery is a signal to invest in encoding, not more cards. Later study and professional life rarely run on flashcards alone.

task.do: Audit 10 of your own cards (or 10 facts you might card). Label each Keep (true reference/evidence worth spaced reps) or Map/Encode instead. Rewrite 2 Keep prompts to vary the cue — about 8–10 minutes.
task.capture: Keep vs Map counts, plus the two rewritten prompts.

check.q: If most items were better as Map/Encode, what should change in your study this week?
check.rubric: correct: Stop carding everything; encode relationships; card sparingly for suitable targets. mostly_correct: Fewer cards vaguely. incorrect: Card every syllabus sentence; ignore PACER; increase new cards.
check.exemplar: I should stop turning everything into cards, encode relationships on a map, and card only the keep-worthy reference/evidence items.

check.q: If you feel overwhelmed by reviews, what does that signal mean according to this lesson?
check.rubric: correct: Invest in encoding and shrink the deck — not add more cards or trust recognition flipping. mostly_correct: Reduce load vaguely. incorrect: Add more cards until better; delete all retrieval.
check.exemplar: Overwhelm signals I should encode better and shrink the deck — not create more cards or catch up by recognition flipping.

check.q: Looking at your two rewritten prompts, what features make a rewritten Keep card match good card use?
check.rubric: correct: Varied cue, answer-before-flip, keep-worthy reference/evidence target; not answer-on-front, multi-idea paragraphs, or saturated clones. mostly_correct: Mentions varying cue only. incorrect: Celebrates answer-visible or saturated identical stems.
check.exemplar: A strong rewrite uses a varied cue I answer before flipping on a true keep-worthy fact — not the answer on the front or another clone of a saturated stem.

days.review: Put it together on your real workload: a simple day/week/month-style schedule, high-quality retrieval in each slot, a debt check so the deck cannot explode, and encoding support so spacing stays a beginning — not the whole system. Sustainability beats heroic card counts.

task.do: For one active course: (1) list topics due for review in the next week, (2) assign each a retrieval method (free / varied-cue / exam-style), (3) cap new cards for the next 3 days at a number you can actually finish, (4) schedule one encoding/map session for the heaviest topic — about 10 minutes.
task.capture: Weekly review list with methods, your new-card cap, and the encoding session time.

check.q: Why does capping new cards align with this subject, given what you planned?
check.rubric: correct: Unbounded new cards create learning debt that collapses the system. mostly_correct: Caps help workload vaguely. incorrect: Caps always reduce learning; software makes caps unnecessary; never card reference facts.
check.exemplar: Capping new cards prevents committing future reps faster than I can repay them. Unbounded additions create learning debt that collapses the system.

check.q: Which weekly slot in your plan best reflects "quality > algorithm," and what would a low-quality slot look like instead?
check.rubric: correct: Dated exam-style/integrated retrieval; contrasts with interval fiddling, passive rereads, or adding without reviewing. mostly_correct: Points to a review without quality contrast. incorrect: Opening app only to tweak settings as the quality win.
check.exemplar: My exam-style retrieval on a dated topic reflects quality over algorithm. Opening the app only to change interval settings or rereading while scrolling would be low quality.

check.q: You scheduled an encoding session beside reviews. What role does that session play relative to spacing?
check.rubric: correct: Flattens forgetting so spacing needs fewer reps — spacing supports encoding rather than replacing it. mostly_correct: Says encoding helps vaguely. incorrect: Proves flashcards are the entire system; means skip all future retrieval.
check.exemplar: Encoding flattens forgetting so I need fewer spaced reps. Spacing supports that encoding — it does not replace it or make flashcards the whole system.

days.review: Checkpoint with fresh material: measure decay, schedule spaced retrieval, demand session quality, detect learning debt, and prefer encoding when decks bloat. Judge the plans and attempts you produce today — not definitions of Ebbinghaus.

task.do: Pick a topic unused in this subject's tasks. Closed recall to estimate retention; book the next 1-day and 1-week retrievals; run a 5-minute high-quality review now; note one card/list item to prune or not create.
task.capture: % estimate, two future dates, what you produced in the 5-minute review, and the prune decision.

check.q: Your retention estimate may have been modest, yet you booked future retrievals. Why is that the right move?
check.rubric: correct: Well-timed reviews slow the next fade — decay is data, not a stop sign. mostly_correct: Says keep going vaguely. incorrect: Low retention means spacing never works; only schedule when memory is perfect.
check.exemplar: Modest retention is decay data, not a stop sign. Booking well-timed retrievals is how I slow the next fade.

check.q: Justify your prune-or-not-create decision using encoding and learning debt.
check.rubric: correct: If encoding/map/explain already carries it, extra card debt is unnecessary; keep items still failing in use. mostly_correct: Mentions pruning without encoding/debt link. incorrect: Pruning always wrong; only delete failing cards; apps forbid pruning.
check.exemplar: I pruned an item my map already explains so I do not add unnecessary card debt. Encoding that carries the idea means I do not need another isolate in the queue.

check.q: What about your 5-minute review shows you avoided the isolated-card trap?
check.rubric: correct: Connected production or exam-like use, not only atomic recognition nods. mostly_correct: Mentions retrieval without integration. incorrect: Faster saturated stems; adding many new isolates; only optimizing interval slider.
check.exemplar: I had to produce a connected explanation/use of the topic, not just nod at atomic cards. That is what avoids shallow spaced mastery.
